I've used OpenBSD the last year or so (as a bastion/jump host for a few systems) after using *BSD systems very little for probably the past decade, and... good lord I love it so much.

Say what you want about the benefits of systemd or the usefulness of other parts of what is now unavoidable with Linux, and I won't argue with many of them, but OpenBSD just feels like a *nix system is supposed to. `ps aux` is like 10 entries at first. `pf` makes so much sense. `man` pages are consistently incredible. It's not and will probably never be a daily driver for me and it may not fit your use case for anything, but I highly recommend playing with it.

item.title: Apple broke an essential presentation feature of iPads
item.description:
Source: teddysvoronos.com

Top Comment:

So I could see the other argument here: I’m presenting from a presentation, I want to switch to a live demo environment, and to do so I need to turn off the presentation entirely?

Now, another operating system might see this tension and say: why not have a UI element come up, and ask the user whether they want to share their entire screen or stay on the existing shared window?

Here, I think this hits a fundamental weakness in Apple’s design culture: if you want to make things magical by removing options from users, occasionally you’re going to hit something that’s impossible to do without giving the user control. And if anything, Apple’s culture has been overtuned towards not providing that control, if at all possible.

Nobody wants complexity for complexity’s sake, but this is the type of thing that should have come up in a meeting, and someone didn’t feel empowered to bring it up.

item.title: France's supermarket fridges were vulnerable online for months
item.description:
Source: ipinfo.io

Related: Hackers activate automatic defrosting in supermarket fridges across Europe - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50055304 - Oct 2026 (1007 comments)

Top Comment:

So the author charitably calls the 2025 vulnerability a "login bypass", but it's much worse than that. The firmware included a "datetime-based password" mechanism: a built-in backdoor password, like it's the 90s again.

The original researcher published about this in August of this year [1], a year after reporting it, titling the report "Defrost the Food", which the attackers apparently took to be a good suggestion.

As the firmware is open for anyone to download [2], blurring the affected function seems more like an invitation to find out more. I know I was curious when the news about the fridges in France broke. The function's actually called "check_code_of_the_day", and this is the implementation:

  uchar check_code_of_the_day(LPCTSTR pass) {
    uchar uVar1;
    LPCTSTR pass_local;
    DATE_STRUCT date;
    INT32 tothex;
    INT32 hex;
    UTF8_STR buff;

    Get_syst_current_tds(&date);
    ftext_s(buff,0x1ff,"%02d%02d%02d%02d",date.month,date.day,date.year,date.month);
    sscanf(buff,"%lx",&tothex);
    ftext_s(buff,0x1ff,,date.day);
    sscanf(buff,"%lx",&hex);
    tothex = __aeabi_idiv(tothex,hex);
    ftext_s(buff,0x1ff,"%05ld",tothex % 100000);
    if ((((*pass == buff[0]) && (pass[1] == buff[1])) && (pass[2] == buff[2])) &&
       ((pass[3] == buff[3] && (pass[4] == buff[4])))) {
      uVar1 = '\x01';
    }
    else {
      uVar1 = '\0';
    }
    return uVar1;
  }
[1] https://www.claroty.com/team82/research/freeze-the-controlle...

[2] https://www.danfoss.com/en-us/service-and-support/downloads/...
